records.sourceFile: Physiological and biomechanical monitoring in American football players - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Nocera A, Sbrollini A, Romagnoli S, Morettini M, Gambi E, Burattini L. Physiological and biomechanical monitoring in American football players: a scoping review. Sensors. 2023;23:3538.
paper.abstract: This scoping review maps biomedical engineering research in American football, screening 1629 records and including 112 studies in topics such as concussion biomechanics, footwear, injury prediction, heat monitoring and training load. Safety-driven work on helmets and footwear dominates, and performance-driven work covers training-load monitoring and catch and kick aerodynamics. The authors identify gaps in internal load monitoring and in shoulder pad innovation.
paper.tldr: This PRISMA scoping review of 112 studies finds most work on concussion biomechanics and training-load monitoring, with little on internal load or shoulder pads. The map shows where wearable monitoring has been applied, but most included studies are laboratory or small-sample sports science.
paper.methods: PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus were searched from 1995 to July 2022 following PRISMA and scoping review guidance, and 1629 records were screened down to 112 research studies in American football players. Studies were classified by topic and design, appraised with design-specific checklists, and tabulated by sample, aim, outcome and quality score.
paper.findings: Concussion biomechanics was the largest topic (55 studies, including 18 head impact telemetry and 16 laboratory reconstruction studies), and in one telemetry cohort head impacts were skewed toward low severity, with a median peak linear acceleration of 20.5 g. Training-load studies (25) measured external load in all cases and internal load in eight, and four papers by Flatt et al. (2018 to 2021) reported heart rate variability (vagal tone) falling across the season in linemen. In injury prediction (8 studies), one preseason model reported sensitivity 0.79 and specificity 0.83 at a threshold of 21 touches on the upper extremity stability test, while two Y-balance test studies gave conflicting results.
paper.limitations: The review notes that its keyword choices and exclusion criteria may have removed relevant papers, and that the injury prediction studies were small and not internally validated. Its own counts disagree in places: heat monitoring is given as 8 in the abstract but 9 studies are listed in the body, and the total of 112 matches the body count. Table 9 labels the prediction-model studies 'High Bias', and the review states that the contradictory injury prediction results were tested on small samples.
paper.practicalImplications: Helmet and footwear claims in this review rest mainly on laboratory and simulation tests, so staff should read them as lab results rather than field outcomes. For load monitoring, the review supports tracking external load with wearables and heart rate variability as an emerging internal load measure, but it finds internal load work limited. Injury prediction tests from the review should not be used alone for screening decisions, given their small samples and contradictory results.
paper.athleteDev: The training-load studies in this review track external load such as distance, speed zones and accelerometer player load, and one group's heart rate variability work reports declining vagal tone in linemen across the season. The review does not link these measures to better on-field performance, so performance benefit remains untested.
paper.rtp: The review does not give return-to-play criteria. One study cited in the review found that head impact biomechanics were not associated with symptom resolution or return-to-play time, so impact data alone should not set return-to-play timing. The review's heart rate variability work includes a single concussed player case report, which cannot guide return to play.

records.sourceFile: Plasma myoglobin indicates muscle damage associated with acceleration-deceleration during football.pdf

paper.citation: Saita Y, Hattori K, Hokari A, Ohyama T, Inoue J, Nishimura T, et al. Plasma myoglobin indicates muscle damage associated with acceleration/deceleration during football. The Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2023;63.
paper.abstract: Fifteen male professional football players had fingertip myoglobin, laboratory creatine kinase and GPS load measured before one official match and at 2, 16 and 40 h afterwards. Myoglobin peaked at 2 h and was most strongly associated with acceleration and deceleration metrics rather than sprint or high-speed running distance. Creatine kinase rose after the match but did not reach statistical significance.
paper.tldr: In 15 male professional footballers after one match, fingertip myoglobin peaked at 2 h and tracked acceleration and deceleration counts, while CK did not change significantly. The study is small, observational and from one club, and it does not test recovery or performance outcomes.
paper.methods: Whole-blood myoglobin was measured with the portable IA-100 immunoassay at baseline and at 2, 16 and 40 h after one official match, and CK was measured in a clinical laboratory. GPS (Catapult Vector X7) recorded total distance, high-speed running, sprint distance, accelerations, decelerations and PlayerLoad for 15 field players. Repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests compared time points, and partial correlations adjusted for baseline linked GPS metrics to myoglobin and CK.
paper.findings: Mean myoglobin was 38.3 ng/mL at baseline, 140.1 at 2 h, 61.9 at 16 h and 43.2 at 40 h (95% CIs given in the text), and only the 2 h value differed significantly from the other time points; three players remained more than 1.5-fold above baseline at 16 h and one at 40 h. CK rose to a mean of 1188.3 U/L at 2 h from 234.3 at baseline, but no time point differed significantly. At 2 h, myoglobin correlated with accelerations (r = 0.87), total distance (0.82), decelerations (0.81) and total PlayerLoad (0.78), while high-speed running (0.66) and sprint distance (0.58) were not significant; CK at 2 h and 16 h correlated only with accelerations (r = 0.77 and 0.76).
paper.limitations: The study covers one club, 15 players and one match, and it measured no physical performance or recovery outcome. Playing time ranged from 10 to 90 minutes, and correlations were adjusted only for baseline biomarker values, so volume of play may drive the associations; total distance (0.82) correlated almost as strongly as accelerations, and the difference from high-speed running was not tested formally. The authors describe myoglobin as back to baseline within 16 h, but the 16 h mean (61.9 ng/mL against 38.3) was only not significantly different, and the Results report full-match distance for five players although the Methods list six full-time players.
paper.practicalImplications: Post-match myoglobin tracked acceleration and deceleration load in these players, so it may be worth testing alongside GPS as a check on post-match muscle damage. The study did not measure recovery, readiness or performance, so it does not show that myoglobin should guide return to training.
paper.athleteDev: In these players, acceleration and deceleration counts were correlated with post-match myoglobin, while high-speed running and sprint distance were not marked significant, which suggests that load monitoring could include these acceleration metrics. The study did not measure physical performance, so any link to lower performance is untested.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It measured post-match muscle damage in squad players and did not address injured athletes, return-to-play criteria or clearance.

records.sourceFile: Playerload Variables are Sensitive        to Changes in Direction and Not Related to Collision Workloads in   Rugby      League Match-Play.pdf

paper.citation: Hulin BT, Gabbett TJ, Johnston RD, Jenkins DG. PlayerLoad variables are sensitive to changes in direction and not related to collision workloads in rugby league match-play. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018.
paper.abstract: Examines how change-of-direction workload and collision workload relate to PlayerLoad variables, using three 60 m drill protocols in junior players and match-play collision and distance data from professional rugby league players. The authors report that PlayerLoad variables rose with change-of-direction demands and were distinct from collision counts, but related strongly to total distance.
paper.tldr: In rugby league, PlayerLoad variables rise when players change direction more often and track total distance closely, while relating only moderately to collision counts. The authors conclude that no PlayerLoad variable is a valid stand-alone measure of collision workload.
paper.methods: Part one: 16 junior players (age 16.8 years) completed three crossover drills of 10 repetitions of 60 m in 15 s, with 0, 1 or 3 changes of direction, and changes of direction were compared by factorial ANOVA with Cohen d effect sizes. Part two: 25 professional players (270 appearances) wore GPS-based microtechnology, and collisions (12,039 events, detected with a device algorithm) were correlated with PlayerLoad variables and distance using Pearson correlations and R2. Two players were excluded from part one for repetitions faster than 15 s.
paper.findings: In part one, PlayerLoad per minute was greater with three changes of direction than straight running (PLVM d=1.50, large; PL2D d=1.38, large; PLSLOW d=1.69, large), and PLSLOW was the only variable with a large difference from one change of direction to three (d=1.29). In part two, collisions per minute correlated with PLVM (R2 0.30, r=0.55) and PL2D (R2 0.37, r=0.61) at distinct levels below R2 0.50, while total distance per minute correlated with PLVM at R2 0.62 (r=0.79, very large).
paper.limitations: Part one used 16 junior players in a controlled drill, and the authors did not test progressive increases in collision demand. In part two, collision counts came from a device algorithm (cited as detecting 97.6% of collisions in an earlier study), not video, and the R2 below 0.50 criterion for 'distinct' relationships is an interpretive threshold. The accepted manuscript has no printed volume or page numbers, so the final citation details need checking against the published issue.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff monitoring rugby league should not use a PlayerLoad total as a measure of collision or contact load on its own, because it rises with change-of-direction demands. For change-of-direction work, the authors suggest PLML and PLV over PLAP and PL2D, and PLSLOW was most sensitive to change of direction but also tracks contact and wrestling at low speed, so it should be interpreted with collision counts.
paper.athleteDev: In junior players, PlayerLoad variables increased with change-of-direction demands at matched distance, so they may help quantify change-of-direction work in training. The study does not show that these measures improve performance or training outcomes.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: the study measured external workload in players and did not examine injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Pooled Versus Individualized Load–Velocity Profiling in the Free-Weight Back Squat and Power Clean.pdf

paper.citation: Thompson SW, Rogerson D, Ruddock A, Banyard HG, Barnes A. Pooled Versus Individualized Load-Velocity Profiling in the Free-Weight Back Squat and Power Clean. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2021 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Ten competitive weightlifters completed 1RM tests and three incremental load-velocity profiles in the back squat and power clean, with mean and peak velocity measured by a linear position transducer. The authors compared pooled and individualized profiles, linear and second-order polynomial fits, and between-subject variability and within-subject reliability at each relative load.
paper.tldr: Load-velocity relationships varied widely between lifters, especially in the back squat. Individualized profiles were more strongly correlated than pooled profiles, and the power clean was reliable across loads while the back squat was not at heavier loads.
paper.methods: Within-subject repeated-measures design with four sessions 48 to 72 hours apart: 1RM testing in each lift, then three profiles at 30-100% of 1RM. GymAware recorded mean and peak velocity per repetition; linear and second-order polynomial models were fitted to pooled and individual data, and reliability was assessed with CV, ICC, typical error and limits of agreement.
paper.findings: Pooled and individualized profiles both showed strong inverse load-velocity relationships, and individualized profiles gave stronger correlations. Between-subject CVs were 8.2-27.8% in the back squat and 4.6-8.5% in the power clean. The power clean met the a priori reliability criteria (ICC above .70, CV below 10%) at all loads, while the back squat did not at heavier loads (MV at 95% or more, PV at 90% or more of 1RM); linear and polynomial models did not differ significantly (back squat P = .45, power clean P = .50).
paper.limitations: Only 10 athletes (2 women) were tested in one laboratory with one transducer. The abstract gives back squat CVs of 13.1-20.5% for loads of 90% of 1RM or more, while the Results give the thresholds as 95% or more for MV (13.1-20.6%) and 90% or more for PV (11.8-15.6%). The claim that individualized profiles are preferable rests on correlation size and reliability rather than a direct test of pooled against individual profiles.
paper.practicalImplications: If profiling is used, the paper supports building an individual profile for each athlete and reading velocity changes against the reported smallest worthwhile change values (for example, 0.02 m/s MV in the back squat). For the back squat, the authors suggest using MV across 30-90% of 1RM rather than heavy-load velocities, and they advise keeping 1RM testing alongside profiling because of time and logistics.
paper.athleteDev: Usable for monitoring strength-speed status in weightlifting-style training, using individual profiles and the reported smallest worthwhile change values. Power clean velocities were reliable across loads, while heavy back squat velocities were not and should not be used to judge progress.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study tested healthy weightlifters and measured no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-training outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Precision of 7 Commercially Available Devices for Predicting the Bench Press 1-Repetition Maximum From the Individual Load-Velocity Relationship.pdf

paper.citation: Pérez-Castilla A, Piepoli A, Garrido-Blanca G, Delgado-García G, Balsalobre-Fernández C, García-Ramos A. Precision of 7 Commercially Available Devices for Predicting the Bench Press 1-Repetition Maximum From the Individual Load-Velocity Relationship. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019.
paper.abstract: Eleven men performed an incremental Smith machine bench press test at 45, 55, 65, 75 and 85% 1RM, followed by 1RM attempts. Seven commercial devices measured mean velocity, and 1RM was predicted from the individual load-velocity relationship using 5 loads or only 2 loads. Five devices (T-Force, Chronojump, Speed4Lift, Velowin and PowerLift) gave acceptable and comparable estimates, while the PUSH band and especially the Beast sensor were less accurate.
paper.tldr: For Smith machine bench press, five of the seven devices estimated 1RM accurately from velocity, and two loads (45% and 85% 1RM) were as accurate as five. The two inertial sensors tested were the least accurate.
paper.methods: Participants completed two sessions 48-72 h apart. Session 1 measured anthropometrics and 1RM. In session 2, they performed 3 repetitions at each of the 5 loads followed by 1RM attempts, with all seven devices recording at the same time. Accuracy was assessed with paired t-tests, Hedges' g, Pearson's r, standard error of the estimate and a device by method ANOVA on absolute errors.
paper.findings: Five devices (T-Force, Chronojump, Speed4Lift, Velowin, PowerLift) showed ES <= 0.40, r >= 0.94 and SEE <= 4.46 kg with both methods, although all except Chronojump significantly overestimated the actual 1RM (Table 1, p 0.001 to 0.045; small ES). PUSH band (ES 0.70-0.83, r 0.93-0.94, SEE 4.45-4.80 kg) significantly underestimated 1RM, and Beast sensor had the lowest accuracy (ES 0.36-0.84, r 0.50-0.68, SEE 9.44-11.2 kg). The ANOVA on absolute errors found a main effect of device (p < 0.001) but no effect of method (p = 0.609).
paper.limitations: The authors state no limitations section. Inference: the sample was 11 men experienced with the bench press, tested on a concentric-only Smith machine bench press with 1RM estimated at a fixed velocity of 0.17 m/s, so results may not transfer to free-weight or touch-and-go lifting, other exercises, women or trained athletes. Even the better devices showed small but significant systematic overestimation of 1RM.
paper.practicalImplications: On a concentric-only Smith machine bench press, T-Force, Chronojump, Speed4Lift, Velowin or PowerLift can estimate 1RM from the velocity at about 45% and 85% 1RM, with the two-point method as accurate as five loads in this sample. Expect small overestimates of a few kilograms with most of these devices, and the authors conclude the PUSH band and Beast sensor are not accurate enough for this use.
paper.athleteDev: Staff wanting a quick 1RM estimate for bench press can use the two-point method (45% and 85% 1RM) with the five devices the paper supports. The study measured prediction accuracy only and did not test training outcomes.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested men on a Smith machine bench press and reports no injured participants or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Predicting Future Perceived    Wellness in Professional Soccer- The Role of Preceding Load and    Wellness.pdf

paper.citation: Jaspers A, Op De Beéck T, Brink MS, Frencken WGP, Staes F, Davis JJ, et al. Predicting Future Perceived Wellness in Professional Soccer: The Role of Preceding Load and Wellness. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019.
paper.abstract: The authors used gradient boosted regression trees to predict next-day perceived wellness (fatigue, sleep quality, muscle soreness, stress and mood) in professional male soccer players over one season. Predictors were GPS external load, session RPE internal load and pre-session wellness, summed over 1 to 7 day windows. Models with pre-session wellness plus load beat a per-player average baseline for fatigue, soreness, stress and mood, while load alone and cumulative load gave no meaningful gain.
paper.tldr: Pre-session wellness combined with recent training or match load gave the best next-day wellness predictions in professional soccer players, but the gains over a player's own average were small. Load alone and cumulative load added little.
paper.methods: Data came from 26 professional male players in the 2015-2016 season, using 10 Hz GPS and accelerometry, session RPE and a five-item morning wellness questionnaire. Each player had an individual gradient boosted regression tree model trained on the first 80% of their data and tested on the last 20%, compared with a baseline of the player's own mean. Models were built for 14 players with at least 80 usable instances, and missing pre-session wellness was filled with the value from two days earlier.
paper.findings: Pre-session wellness combined with external and/or internal load gave small effect sizes over baseline for fatigue, muscle soreness and stress levels across most time frames. For mood, only acute external load with pre-session wellness and the three-way combination gave a small effect. External load, internal load and their combination alone gave trivial effect sizes, cumulative load did not improve prediction, and sleep quality was trivial for almost all models.
paper.limitations: The abstract says only the combination of external load, internal load and pre-session wellness gave non-trivial effects, but the Discussion reports small effects for pre-session wellness combined with either load measure alone. The Discussion states the models beat 'average player thresholds', but the baseline was each player's own average, so no threshold comparison was tested. The effect-size values appear only in figures not present in the text, match and rest days are excluded, and the direction of effects is not reported.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that daily pre-session wellness alongside GPS and session RPE may help predict next-day fatigue, soreness and stress in a squad. They also suggest comparing predicted and reported wellness to flag players for closer review, but the study did not test whether this changes training decisions. Sleep quality was poorly predicted and mood only in some combinations, so the models add little for those items, although the authors still regard them as useful for assessing a player's status.
paper.athleteDev: Staff could use daily wellness scores with load data to flag players whose reported wellness falls outside their predicted range for closer review. The paper does not show the direction of load effects or that acting on predictions improves performance, so it cannot set individual load targets.
paper.rtp: The study has no injury or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The authors also state that the wellness questionnaire's reliability and validity have not been extensively studied.

records.sourceFile: Preseason screen cannot predict injury over three years of college football.pdf

paper.citation: Mortensen BB, Mitchell UH, Johnson AW, Fellingham GW, Feland JB, Myrer JW. Preseason Screen Cannot Predict Injury over Three Years of College Football. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2020;52(11):2286-2292.
paper.abstract: Functional Movement Screen (FMS) total score, item scores and asymmetries were tested as predictors of noncontact injury in 208 NCAA Division I football players over three seasons (343 observations), with analyses by position group and adjustment for exposure. Total score and asymmetries did not predict injury. Push-up stability in the combo group was the only item associated in the expected direction, and rotary stability was associated in the opposite direction for the team and skill group.
paper.tldr: In three seasons of NCAA Division I football, the preseason Functional Movement Screen total score and asymmetry count did not predict noncontact injury. Only one item result (push-up stability in linebackers and tight ends) ran in the expected direction, and rotary stability ran the opposite way, so the screen should not be used alone to judge injury risk.
paper.methods: Three-year prospective descriptive epidemiology study of one NCAA Division I football team. FMS was scored before preseason practice, and noncontact injuries were recorded daily and coded by athletic trainers. Generalized linear mixed models (binomial and Poisson) related FMS total scores, individual item scores and asymmetry counts to injuries by team and position group, with and without adjustment for exposure, using alpha of 0.0167.
paper.findings: Total FMS score was not associated with injury for the team (P = 0.130) or any position group, and asymmetry count was not associated with injury for the team (P = 0.472). Push-up stability was inversely associated with injury in the combo group (P = 0.001), with an estimated injury risk of 13.44% at a score of 2 and 3.67% at a score of 3 (not adjusted for exposure). Rotary stability was positively associated with injury for the team (P < 0.001) and skill group (P = 0.011), the opposite of the expected direction.
paper.limitations: Coaching and strength staff changed across the study, and play volume dropped in year 3 (1,770 plays vs 2,059 and 1,792), which the authors note may have affected FMS scores. Many item-by-group tests were run with alpha set at 0.0167, and the authors note that large samples can produce statistically significant results with little practical meaning. The abstract notes only the push-up stability result as being in the expected direction and does not report the rotary stability results shown in Table 4.
paper.practicalImplications: In this NCAA Division I football sample, preseason FMS total scores and asymmetry counts did not identify athletes at higher noncontact injury risk, so they should not be used alone to screen for injury. Isolated item results, including the rotary stability association in the opposite direction, should be interpreted cautiously. The authors suggest that other assessments be considered or developed.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured injury, not performance, and does not inform performance development.
paper.rtp: The study addresses preseason screening for future noncontact injury, not recovery or return to play, so it cannot guide return-to-play clearance or rehabilitation decisions.

records.sourceFile: Preseason shoulder range of motion screening and in-season risk of shoulder and elbow injuries in overhead athletes- systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Pozzi F, Plummer HA, Shanley E, Thigpen CA, Bauer C, Wilson ML, et al. Preseason shoulder range of motion screening and in-season risk of shoulder and elbow injuries in overhead athletes: systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 prospective cohorts of overhead athletes testing whether preseason shoulder range of motion (ROM) predicts in-season shoulder and elbow injury. Throwing-arm external rotation insufficiency was associated with injury in professional baseball pitchers, while absolute ROM and internal rotation deficit were not pooled as predictors and evidence in other overhead sports was limited.
paper.tldr: In overhead athletes, preseason shoulder range of motion generally did not predict in-season shoulder or elbow injury. The exception was a throwing-arm external rotation shortfall (less than 5 degrees more than the non-throwing arm) in professional baseball pitchers, which rests on three studies.
paper.methods: Systematic review (six databases to September 2018) and random-effects Mantel-Haenszel meta-analysis of prospective cohorts that tracked shoulder and elbow injuries in overhead athletes. Study quality was scored with a modified Downs and Black checklist (mean 14.9 of 21 points, range 11 to 18). Pooled odds or risk ratios were calculated for absolute ROM and ROM deficit variables.
paper.findings: Throwing-arm external rotation insufficiency was associated with injury in pooled data from three professional baseball studies (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.24 to 2.92, P < 0.01; I2 = 0%). Absolute shoulder ROM and internal rotation deficit of 20 degrees or more were not associated with injury, and shoulder flexion deficit of 5 degrees or more was not associated with injury in the pooled analysis. In single studies outside the meta-analysis, absolute external rotation below 93 or above 100 degrees was associated with shoulder injury in 74 swimmers (unadjusted OR 24.9 and 23.0, with very wide confidence intervals), and softball, volleyball and tennis cohorts showed no association.
paper.limitations: Only three studies contributed to each ROM meta-analysis, and heterogeneity was high across age, position, competition level and injury definitions. Four studies did not describe how they selected their sample, only five adjusted for confounders, and the funnel plot suggested missing negative studies for external rotation deficit. The review reports 3,314 athletes enrolled but uses 3,750 (after counting athletes followed over several seasons and loss to follow-up) as the denominator for the 17% injury rate, with different sport counts in each, and most included studies did not adjust for previous injury or exposure.
paper.practicalImplications: For professional baseball pitchers, preseason screening should record whether throwing-arm external rotation is at least 5 degrees greater than the non-throwing arm, since the shortfall was associated with in-season injury (OR 1.90). Absolute shoulder range of motion or internal rotation differences of 20 degrees should not be used alone to flag injury risk. The evidence is too limited to rely on ROM screening in handball, softball, volleyball or tennis, and youth and high school pitchers did not show a consistent association.
paper.athleteDev: The review addresses shoulder and elbow injury risk and does not measure performance, so it does not inform performance development.
paper.rtp: The review did not assess return to play or rehabilitation, so its preseason ROM findings cannot set return-to-throw criteria after injury.

records.sourceFile: Prevalence of carboxy‐ delta8‐tetrahydrocannabiniol in antidoping samples.pdf

paper.citation: Nair VS, Heybroek M, Boyle E, Rogers M, Campbell T, Eichner D, et al. Prevalence of carboxy-Δ8-tetrahydrocannabiniol in antidoping samples. Drug Test Anal. 2024.
paper.abstract: Δ8-THC products have become widely available with little oversight, and a Δ9-THC-COOH assay may overestimate Δ9-THC-COOH if the Δ8 isomer is present and not resolved. This study used LC-MS/MS to separate the Δ8 and Δ9 THC-COOH isomers in 1,000 routine anti-doping samples with a presumptive THC-COOH finding, and reports that about 12% contained Δ8-THC-COOH.
paper.tldr: In 1,000 routine anti-doping urine samples that screened positive for THC-COOH, about 12% (119) also contained Δ8-THC-COOH. Because the samples were limited to screen-positive results, this is not a prevalence of Δ8-THC use across tested athletes.
paper.methods: Routine anti-doping urine samples with a presumptive THC-COOH screen above 5 ng/mL, from Olympic sports (in and out of competition) and professional sports, were reanalysed by a modified LC-MS/MS confirmation method that resolves the Δ8 and Δ9 isomers. The method was validated over 0.5 to 500 ng/mL, with limits of identification of 0.5 ng/mL for both isomers and limits of quantitation of 2 ng/mL (Δ8) and 0.5 ng/mL (Δ9).
paper.findings: Of 1,000 samples with screening concentrations between 5 and 450 ng/mL, 119 contained Δ8-THC-COOH. In these samples, Δ8 made up 5% to 100% of the combined Δ8 and Δ9 isomer signal. The authors note that the screening method does not separate the isomers and therefore measures total THC-COOH.
paper.limitations: Single laboratory and single testing programme, with samples drawn only from those screening positive for THC-COOH. The text gives no athlete numbers, sex, sport or in- versus out-of-competition breakdown, and does not say how many Δ8-positive samples would have exceeded the Δ9-THC-COOH threshold. The abstract describes the 5% to 100% range as a share of total carboxy-THC, while Figure 3 expresses it as a ratio to the sum of the two isomers. The conclusion that Δ8-THC use has increased among athletes is not tested by this single time-point dataset, and applying the Δ9 threshold to the sum of both isomers is the authors' proposal, not a tested rule.
paper.practicalImplications: Testing programmes that apply Δ9-THC-COOH thresholds may need an isomer-resolving method, because a screen can overstate Δ9-THC-COOH when Δ8 is present. The authors state that rules for reporting Δ8-THC-COOH are unclear, so programmes need their own written policy for it.
paper.athleteDev: The paper reports no performance outcomes and has no direct use for training or performance decisions. Its relevance to performance staff is awareness that Δ8-THC products are in use and that Δ9-only testing cannot separate the isomers.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address return to sport, injury or clinical care. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions, and the authors state that the potential for abuse or side effects is outside the scope of the study.

records.sourceFile: Protocol standardization may improve precision error of InBody 720 body composition analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Herberts T, Slater GJ, Farley A, Hogarth L, Areta JL, Paulsen G, et al. Protocol standardization may improve precision error of InBody 720 body composition analysis. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2023 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Eighteen recreational athletes (10 men, 8 women) completed two within-day and one between-day InBody 720 bioelectrical impedance scans, with diet and physical activity replicated over the 24 hours before the first scan. Within- and between-day precision error did not differ significantly for fat-free mass, fat mass or total body water. The authors conclude that 24-hour standardization may minimize precision error, but the study has no unstandardized comparison day.
paper.tldr: After 24-hour diet and activity replication, the gap between within-day and between-day precision error was within the 1% bound for fat-free mass and total body water, but not for fat mass. Without a comparison day, the study cannot show that this standardization beats current best practice.
paper.methods: Test-retest study in 18 healthy recreationally active adults (10 men, 8 women, aged 18-40 years). Each participant had two consecutive within-day InBody 720 scans and a third scan on a randomly assigned day before or after, with food and activity from the 24 hours before the first scan replicated the next day and recorded in diaries. Precision was expressed as RMS-SD, %CV and least significant change (2.77 x RMS-SD), with paired t tests (alpha .025) and two one-sided equivalence tests using a 1% bound.
paper.findings: Within-day RMS-SD was 411 g for FFM and 400 g for FM, and between-day LSC was 1,243 g for FFM, 1,053 g for FM and 881 ml for TBW. Within- and between-day %CV did not differ significantly (FFM p = .36, FM p = .82, TBW p = .20). The equivalence tests placed the difference in %CV inside the 1% bound for FFM (delta 0.14, 95% CI -0.013 to 0.29) and TBW (delta 0.17, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.48), but not for FM (delta 0.20, 95% CI -1.71 to 2.11). The diet diaries showed no significant difference in energy or macronutrient intake between the two days.
paper.limitations: There was no randomized or unstandardized comparison day, so the authors state that effectiveness versus best practice cannot be concluded. Eighteen participants is below the ISCD-recommended 30 for LSC, diet was self-replicated, incidental activity was not recorded, and menstrual status and posture were not controlled. The results text describes the FFM and TBW confidence intervals as 'exceeding' the 1% bound although they lie inside it (upper limits 0.29 and 0.48), and the discussion quotes different upper limits (0.365%, 0.437%, and 2.143% for FM), so exact values should be checked against Figure 3.
paper.practicalImplications: A 24-hour diet and training diary is a low-cost option practitioners can trial before InBody scans, although this study did not compare it against usual preparation. Fat-mass precision was poorer than FFM or TBW (%CV about 3.2 to 3.4%) and its between-day difference could not be shown to be within the 1% bound, so fat-mass change should be read against the reported between-day LSC of about 1,053 g.
paper.athleteDev: The paper addresses measurement precision in recreational athletes, not training or performance. It can inform how body-composition change is tracked, but it does not show that changes in body composition improve performance.
paper.rtp: The sample was healthy recreational athletes, and the study does not include injured athletes or return-to-play decisions. Its data should not be used to judge readiness to return to sport or to set body-composition targets for returning athletes.

records.sourceFile: Pyjamas, polysomnography and professional athletes - The role of sleep tracking technology in sport.pdf

paper.citation: Driller MW, Dunican IC, Omond SET, Boukhris O, Stevenson S, Lambing K, et al. Pyjamas, Polysomnography and Professional Athletes: The Role of Sleep Tracking Technology in Sport. Sports. 2023;11:14.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarizes the importance of sleep for athletes, the sleep-monitoring tools used in sport, and the reliability and validity of sleep trackers. It also covers the limitations of trackers, their use to guide behaviour change, and practical recommendations for practitioners.
paper.tldr: Consumer sleep trackers are reasonably good at estimating total sleep duration but are weak at detecting wake and sleep stages. The review advises choosing a tool to fit the monitoring goal and reading trends over at least 7 to 28 nights.
paper.methods: Narrative review of polysomnography and home sleep tests, wrist-, finger- and head-worn wearables, nearables, smart pyjamas, questionnaires and diaries, and the sleep metrics trackers report, with a table comparing tools. No systematic search or inclusion criteria are described.
paper.findings: Wearables were sensitive for sleep periods (91-96%) but had low specificity for wake (18% to 80%, averaging about 50%) against polysomnography, and a 2020 expert consensus was cited as finding insufficient evidence for accurate sleep staging by commercial wearables. Device-level figures varied: the Oura ring showed 96% sensitivity for sleep, with agreement of 65%, 51% and 61% for light, deep and REM sleep; the Somfit head-worn device correctly classified 92% of sleep epochs and 57% of wake epochs (kappa 0.48). The Phyjama smart pyjamas have been validated for sleeping position but not yet for sleep metrics.
paper.limitations: No search strategy or inclusion criteria are described, and the review does not grade the strength of the evidence it cites. The Dreem accuracy figure comes from a manufacturer validation, and the review notes that many algorithms are proprietary, that not all wearables show acceptable agreement with polysomnography, and that validation is lacking for some rings and for smart pyjama sleep metrics. Two authors are employees of Cerebra, a sleep technology start-up, and Table 1 lists the Cerebra Sleep System as an example home polysomnography tool.
paper.practicalImplications: The review recommends wearing a tracker for at least 7 nights, and preferably 2 to 3 weeks, and reading rolling averages over 14, 21 or 28 nights. It suggests using wearables mainly for duration and timing trends and not for stage data, and using polysomnography for sleep-disorder diagnosis. It also cautions against proprietary readiness scores and notes that feedback can be turned off around key competitions.
paper.athleteDev: Sleep trackers can show trends in sleep duration and timing across a squad or season, and the review presents them mainly as an awareness tool for behaviour change. Stage data and proprietary readiness scores are not validated enough to set training or competition decisions. The review cites a sham-feedback study in people with insomnia (not athletes) showing that falsely reported poor sleep impaired daytime cognition. In professional rugby league players, a sleep-hygiene seminar gave about 20 minutes more sleep, but this had returned to baseline a month later.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport, injury or clinical clearance, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It cautions against using tracker readiness or recovery scores for elite athletes because these measures are often unvalidated.
